rubric_diagnosis: Both instructions measure the formatting pattern alone; neither smuggles in an effectiveness judgement. Instance 2 is an explicit tally ('Count the fraction...', 'note literal repetition'), and instance 1 scores on presence/density ('Score high when the prose uses many short standalone lines... abrupt visual breaks'). Nothing asks whether the fragmentation earns its place, sets a beat, or serves the story. The study already carries the craft twin on the A-side ('Controlled Repetition and Rhythm', which requires patterning be CONTROLLED and do rhetorical work), and its shallow counting probe ('Repeated-phrase exact-match count') was independently routed nuisance -- the same surface/craft cut this channel falls on.
deciding_phrase: Count the fraction of paragraphs that are a single short clause or sentence (under roughly eight words) set off by its own line break
reason: The reviewer is right that lineation can be technique and wrong that this criterion measures it. As written, both instances count typographic density, pooling deliberate fragmentation with fashion-imitation and careless writing; the deliberate subset is never identified, so no single latent cause is being fingerprinted -- that is what surface-only means. 'Deliberate stylistic control' would be the parent only if the instruction separated controlled from uncontrolled breaks; the A-side criterion does that, this one does not. With no parent, nothing co-causes better writing: mixed=false. Instance 2's .5816 AUC, the highest of 54 nuisance channels, is what a strong nuisance looks like, not evidence of quality. Two proposer families, two blind auditors (.75/.80), same verdict.
